panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: The radiograph shows the AP view of a 5-year-old patient, clearly demonstrating the 'wafer-thin' or sclerotic appearance of the navicular bone, which is typical of Kohler disease. B: The lateral radiograph of the right foot shows both the sclerotic navicular and the inconsistently fragmented medial cuneiform, consistent with Kohler disease.
panels.attribution_text: Holley et al. Kohler Disease With Concurrent Avascular Necrosis of the Medial Cuneiform: A Report of Two Cases.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.89411. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Radiographs from Patient 1’s initial visit, including anteroposterior (A) and lateral (B) views of the right foot of the five-year-old patient; note the “wafer-thin” (i.e., thin, sclerotic) appearance of the navicular, typical of Kohler disease, and the inconsistently fragmented appearance of the medial cuneiform.
in_text_mentions: At his first visit with the pediatric orthopedic surgeon, a physical exam showed no obvious deformity or ecchymosis present about the midfoot; however, he had notable tenderness to palpation over the navicular bone. The patient was neurovascularly intact with a normal range of motion of the bilateral lower extremities. The patient had difficulty with ambulation due to pain. Repeat radiographs (Figure 1) were obtained of the right foot at that time, which revealed avascular necrosis of the navicular with associated avascular necrosis of the medial cuneiform.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: The radiograph shows the AP view of the foot demonstrating uniform sclerosis and progressive ossification of the navicular, which is consistent with bone healing in Kohler disease. B: The radiograph shows the lateral view of the foot demonstrating progressive ossification and bone healing of the navicular, consistent with the progression of Kohler disease.

panels.figure_caption: Anterior-posterior (A) and lateral (B) view radiographs were obtained eight weeks after initial diagnosis. Images demonstrate bone healing with uniform sclerosis and progressive ossification of the navicular and medial cuneiform.
in_text_mentions: The patient was treated conservatively in a walking boot with reduced activity and weight-bearing status. He was re-evaluated at the pediatric orthopedic clinic approximately eight weeks following initial diagnosis, and repeat radiographs were obtained (Figure 4). The patient was accompanied by his mother, who noted resolution of the patient’s pain. He was then made weight-bearing as tolerated and released for activity without restrictions.
